title: Arrhenius acid
content: Arrhenius acid is any substance that dissociates to produce hydrogen ions (H^+) when it dissolves in water.
e: An Arrhenius acid dissociates in water to give hydrogen ions, H+. The definition only works in aqueous solution.

title: Arrhenius base
content: Arrhenius base is any substance that dissociates to produce hydroxide ions (OH^-) when it dissolves in water.
e: An Arrhenius base dissociates in water to give hydroxide ions, OH-. Again the definition is for water solutions.

title: Bronsted-Lowry acid
content: Bronsted-Lowry acid is any substance that can donate a proton.
e: A Bronsted-Lowry acid is a proton donor. It must have a hydrogen it can give away as H+.

title: Bronsted-Lowry base
content: Bronsted-Lowry base is any substance that can accept a proton.
e: A Bronsted-Lowry base is a proton acceptor. It must have a lone pair that can take H+.

title: Conjugate acid
content: Conjugate acid is a species that forms when a base gains a proton.
e: A conjugate acid is the species you get when a base gains a proton. NH4+ is the conjugate acid of NH3.

title: Conjugate base
content: Conjugate base is a species that forms when an acid loses a proton.
e: A conjugate base is the species left when an acid loses a proton. CH3COO- is the conjugate base of ethanoic acid.

title: Conjugate acid-base pair
content: Conjugate acid-base pair is an acid-base pair that consists of either an acid and its conjugate base or a base and its conjugate acid.
e: A conjugate acid-base pair differs by one proton. You always name them as the acid and the base it becomes after losing H+, or the other way round.

title: Lewis acid
content: Lewis acid is any substance that can accept an electron pair.
e: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair. BF3 and H+ both count, even when no proton transfer is written.

title: Lewis base
content: Lewis base is any substance that can donate an electron pair.
e: A Lewis base donates an electron pair. Ammonia is a Lewis base when the nitrogen lone pair binds to H+ or to a metal ion.

title: Autoionisation of water
content: Autoionisation of water is a reaction between two water molecules yielding hydronium and hydroxide ions.
e: Autoionisation of water is two water molecules reacting to give hydronium and hydroxide. That tiny equilibrium is why pure water still has [H+] and [OH-].

title: Amphiprotic molecule
content: Amphiprotic molecule is one which can have both proton-accepting (protophilic) and proton-donating (protogenic) properties.
e: An amphiprotic molecule can donate a proton and also accept a proton. Water and hydrogen carbonate both behave this way.

title: Ionic product of water
content: Ionic product of water is the equilibrium constant for the autoionisation of water which is the product of the molar concentrations of H^+ and OH^- ions at a particular temperature.
e: The ionic product of water, Kw, is [H+][OH-] at a stated temperature. At 25 degrees Celsius it is 1.0 x 10^-14.

title: Neutral aqueous solution
content: Neutral aqueous solution is one in which the concentrations of hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions are equal at the value of 1.0 	imes 10^{-7} 	ext{ mol dm}^{-3} at 25 °C (298 K) (pH = 7).
e: A neutral aqueous solution has [H+] equal to [OH-]. At 25 degrees Celsius that concentration is 1.0 x 10^-7 mol dm^-3, so pH is 7.

title: pH
content: pH is defined as the negative logarithm to base 10 of the molar concentration of the hydrogen ions.
e: pH is the negative logarithm of the hydrogen-ion concentration. Each drop of one pH unit means [H+] has become ten times larger.

title: pOH
content: pOH is defined as the negative logarithm to base 10 of the molar concentration of the hydroxide ions.
e: pOH is the negative logarithm of the hydroxide-ion concentration. At 25 degrees Celsius, pH plus pOH equals 14.

title: Strong acids
content: Strong acids are strong electrolytes that completely ionise in water.
e: Strong acids are strong electrolytes that ionise completely in water. Hydrochloric, nitric, and sulphuric acids are the usual examples.

title: Weak acids
content: Weak acids are weak electrolytes that partially ionise only to a limited extent in water.
e: Weak acids are weak electrolytes that ionise only to a limited extent in water. Ethanoic acid is the usual example, so most of it stays as molecules.

title: Strong bases
content: Strong bases are strong electrolytes that ionise completely in water.
e: Strong bases ionise completely in water. Group 1 hydroxides such as NaOH are the usual examples.

title: Weak bases
content: Weak bases are weak electrolytes that ionise to a very limited extent in water.
e: Weak bases ionise only to a very limited extent in water. Ammonia is the usual example.

title: Basicity of an acid
content: Basicity of an acid is the number of hydrogen ions that one molecule of an acid can produce.
e: Basicity of an acid is how many hydrogen ions one molecule of that acid can produce. H2SO4 is dibasic because one molecule can give two H+.

title: Acidity of a base
content: Acidity of a base is the number of molecules of a monoprotic acid that will neutralise one molecule of the base.
e: Acidity of a base is how many molecules of a monoprotic acid are needed to neutralise one molecule of the base. It counts the OH- or the proton-accepting sites.

title: Acid dissociation constant (K_a)
content: Acid dissociation constant (K_a) is the equilibrium constant for a weak acid.
e: Ka is the equilibrium constant for a weak acid ionising in water. A larger Ka means more ions at equilibrium and a stronger weak acid.

title: Base dissociation constant (K_b)
content: Base dissociation constant (K_b) is the equilibrium constant for a weak base.
e: Kb is the equilibrium constant for a weak base ionising in water. A larger Kb means a stronger weak base.
